messages.author: 3ef7a01c7d912ca2
messages.subject: How to vectorize this?
parts:
I am trying to vectorize the following working code snippet, but could not get the syntax right:

parameters{
  vector[6] cf_raw[3];
  vector<lower=0>[3] cf_mu;
  vector<lower=0>[3] cf_sigma;
}


transformed parameters{
  vector[6] cf[3];
  cf[1]    = cf_mu[1] + cf_sigma[1] * cf_raw[1];
  cf[2]    = cf_mu[2] + cf_sigma[2] * cf_raw[2];
  cf[3]    = cf_mu[3] + cf_sigma[3] * cf_raw[3];
 
  # How to vectorize the above three lines, something like
  # cf    = cf_mu + cf_sigma * cf_raw;
}

Probably it does not given an advantage speedwise with only 3 cfs, but I try to understand the syntax.

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: How to vectorize this?
parts:
I think you need

matrix[3,6] cf_raw; (as param)

matrix[3,6] cf;

cf = rep_matrix(cf_mu, 3) + diag_matrix(cf_sigma) * cf_raw;

For example.

Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to vectorize this?
parts:
> On Dec 21, 2016, at 10:12 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I think you need
>
> matrix[3,6] cf_raw; (as param)
>
> matrix[3,6] cf;
>
> cf = rep_matrix(cf_mu, 3) + diag_matrix(cf_sigma) * cf_raw;

We should put a huge warning on diag_matrix as it's hugely inefficient
in that it fills up a square matrix with zeroes, all of which go on
the autodiff stack. For efficiency, you can use this:

diag_pre_multiply(cf_sigma, cf_raw)

instead of diag_matrix(cf_sigma) * cf_raw. We introduced the more
efficient specialized functions later, but didn't want to remove the
natural ones. When we get a lint mode going, we'll be able to warn people
to rethink uses of diag_matrix automatically.

- Bob

parts:
Dieter,

put it into a loop. Expanding code is no good idea. It eats some cache memory your CPU.

Andre

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: How to vectorize this?
parts:
Expanding code isn't the problem so much as an expanding
expression graph. That can consume a lot of memory in
large models---more than will fit in cache. It's about
40 bytes per subexpression of the log density that gets
evaluated.

- Bob
